title: This Marketing Team's Help Center Videos Used to Take Hours. Now It's 10 Minutes.
intro:
Good Morning Thorium Valley, welcome back to the Catalyst Newsletter.

Today we're talking about a marketing VP who made his team do an AI science fair where everyone had to pick an annoying workflow and fix it, and the simplest project might be the one worth stealing.

We've also got a consulting leader who was so tired of the prep work before every client call that he built an AI clone of himself to do it all, and now five hours of his week just don't exist anymore.

And we're looking at a woman who runs her entire agency solo and figured out how to use a free tool that reads her prospects' body language on calls so she knows exactly what to pitch before she even opens the proposal doc.

stories.title: This Marketing Team's Help Center Videos Used to Take Hours. Now It's 10 Minutes.
stories.content:
Owner.com's VP of Marketing, David Fallarme, did something kind of brilliant. He made his marketing team present AI projects to each other.

He called it an AI science fair, and the format was simple. Everyone picks a workflow that's annoying, builds something with AI to fix it, then shows the team what they made. Three projects came out of it, ranked by difficulty, and the easiest one might be the most useful.

Haley Smith, one of the marketers on the team, tackled help center videos. If you've ever made these, you know the drill. You write a script, record a Loom, re-record it because you fumbled a sentence, edit it, and an hour later you have one video that maybe 40 people will watch. Smith built a custom GPT that takes internal docs and standardizes them into a script, then ran that script through an AI voiceover tool layered on top of a screen recording. New time per video: 10 minutes.

The other two projects were more advanced. Fallarme himself built a workflow that takes sales call recordings, sends customized summaries to Slack through Zapier, converts them to audio with ElevenLabs, and drops the MP3 back in Slack so he can listen to "podcasts" about his sales process while walking his dog. And another teammate built a dashboard you can literally talk to, where you ask Claude questions like "what video got the most engagement on Facebook in October?" and get answers instantly because all the data lives in one place.

The help center video project is the one worth stealing though, because anyone can do it today and the pain it solves is universal.

The Formula

1. Pick your most repetitive video type. Help center explainers, onboarding walkthroughs, feature tutorials, whatever you keep re-recording.

2. Build a custom GPT in Claude (or ChatGPT) with your docs. Upload your internal documentation, style guide, and a couple example scripts.

3. Record your screen doing the walkthrough. No voiceover, no pressure. Just click through the process in silence.

4. Layer AI voiceover on top. Tools like ElevenLabs or Descript can take your script and generate a natural-sounding voiceover.

5. Batch them. Once the system works, knock out five in a sitting.

Have Claude Explain This to Me

Copy this prompt into Claude:

A marketing team at a restaurant tech company was spending hours on each
help center video. They built a custom GPT loaded with internal docs that
converts any documentation into a video script, then layered AI voiceover
onto screen recordings. Total time per video dropped to about 10 minutes.

Here's the basic approach from Thorium Valley:
- Pick your most repetitive video type (tutorials, onboarding, FAQs)
- Build a custom GPT with your docs and style guide to auto-generate scripts
- Record your screen walking through the process with no voiceover
- Use an AI voice tool like ElevenLabs or Descript to narrate the script
  over the recording

stories.title: He Built an AI Agent That Preps All His Client Meetings. It Saves Him 5 Hours a Week.
stories.content:
Dave McCann talks to about ten clients a week.

McCann is a global managing partner at IBM Consulting, responsible for thousands of client relationships including Nestlé, Ericsson, and Riyadh Air. Before every meeting, his team used to spend 30 minutes pulling together a briefing doc and hopping on a prep call. Multiply that by ten meetings and you're looking at five hours a week just getting ready to have conversations.

So he built an AI agent he named after himself. Digital Dave scans his calendar, spots the upcoming client meetings, pulls internal data on project status and services sold, checks external sources like annual reports and market news, and then generates a list of ten things McCann needs to know before walking in.

The part that makes this interesting for everyone else is that McCann's problem is incredibly common. If you manage accounts, run a team, or just have a calendar full of meetings where you're expected to show up informed, you're probably doing some version of this prep work manually.

McCann also freed up three or four staffers who used to spend hours assembling those briefings. They now do other work.

The Formula

1. Build a meeting brief template. Open a Google Doc and write out what you'd actually want to know before any meeting.

2. Create a Claude Project for meeting prep. Paste your brief template into the Project instructions.

3. Feed it what you've got before each meeting. Paste in your last email thread, notes from previous meetings, and recent context.

4. Ask Claude to generate the brief. Something like "Based on everything here, write me a meeting brief using the template."

5. Do this for a week and notice what changes.

Have Claude Explain This to Me

Copy this prompt into Claude:

An executive at IBM Consulting was spending 30 minutes prepping for every
client meeting, times ten meetings a week. He built an AI agent that scans
his calendar, pulls client data, and generates a briefing doc with the ten
most important things he needs to know. It saved him five hours a week and
freed up several staffers from prep work.

Here's the basic approach from Thorium Valley:
- Create a meeting brief template with sections like attendee context,
  last discussion, company news, open questions, and opportunities
- Set up a Claude Project with that template in the instructions
- Before each meeting paste in email threads, past notes, and any
  relevant context about the person or company
- Ask Claude to generate a structured brief you can scan in two minutes

When I paste this, start by saying: "Hey! I have all the context from
Thorium Valley and heard you're trying to automate your meeting prep
with AI. Could I get a little more context on:
1. What kinds of meetings fill up your calendar most often, and what does
   your current prep process look like before those calls?
2. What information do you wish you always had going into a meeting but
   rarely have time to pull together?"

stories.title: She Cut Her Proposal Process From a Week to a Day Using Two Free AI Tools
stories.content:
Adebukola Ajao runs B.D.Y. CONSULT, a full-service marketing agency, completely by herself.

She's done it for a decade. Every client strategy, every creative direction call, every partnership and piece of marketing execution lands on her desk because there is no other desk. That setup works great until you need to write a new client proposal, which used to eat an entire week of her life.

About two years ago she started feeding her discovery call notes, emails, and Google Docs into AI and asking it to draft proposals using templates she'd already built. The whole process now takes a day or less, according to Business Insider.

The part that caught our attention was how she uses Read AI to analyze her prospect calls. It doesn't just transcribe what people said, it picks up on engagement and body language throughout the conversation. So if a prospect leaned in when she mentioned influencer strategy but checked out during the pricing section, she knows exactly which parts of her proposal to double down on.

"If a client says no, I don't feel burned out from having spent a week doing their proposal," Ajao told Business Insider. "It's just onto the next one."

The Formula

1. Record your next client or prospect call. Use Read AI, Otter, or even just Zoom's built-in transcription.

2. Write one reusable proposal template. Lay out the sections you use every time.

3. Paste the transcript and template into Claude. Ask it to fill in the template using what the prospect actually said.

4. Edit the 30% that needs you. Your job is voice, strategy, and the judgment calls.

5. Repeat and refine. Save your best proposals as examples for next time.

Have Claude Explain This to Me

Copy this prompt into Claude:

A solo marketing agency founder was spending over a week writing each client
proposal. She started recording discovery calls, transcribing them with Read
AI, and feeding the transcripts into AI along with her proposal template to
get first drafts back in minutes. Her turnaround dropped from a week to a day.

Here's the basic approach from Thorium Valley:
- Record and transcribe your prospect or client calls
- Build one reusable proposal template with your standard sections
- Paste the transcript and template into Claude to generate a first draft
- Focus your editing time on voice, strategy, and personalization

When I paste this, start by saying: "Hey! I have all the context from
Thorium Valley and heard you're trying to speed up how you write proposals
or client deliverables. Could I get a little more context on:
1. What kind of proposals or documents do you write most often, and roughly
   how long does each one take you right now?
2. What's the part that eats the most time — the research, the first draft,
   or the back-and-forth revisions?"

title: A Window Cleaner Is Using AI as His CFO for $40 a Month
intro:
Good Morning Thorium Valley, welcome back to the Catalyst Newsletter.

Today we're talking about a window cleaner who pays $40 a month for ChatGPT and Claude and uses them like a full finance team, and honestly his approach to prepping for his accountant is something every small business owner should steal.

We're also looking at how one company's engineering team spun up 80 AI agents inside Notion, none of them took more than five minutes to build, and now one guy walks into meetings knowing everything that happened overnight without reading a single Slack thread.

And we've got a CMO who got tired of her team "using AI" without actually changing how they work, so she mapped out 700 daily tasks across her whole marketing org and cut a 50-step campaign process down to 11.

stories.title: A Window Cleaner Is Using AI as His CFO for $40 a Month
stories.content:
Kyle Ray runs a window cleaning company and his entire C-suite is artificial intelligence.

Ray is the founder of Geek Window Cleaning, a side hustle he grew into a six-figure business. He pays $40 a month for ChatGPT and Claude and uses them the way a bigger company would use a finance team. He asks them to surface tax strategies, prep questions for his CPA, and double-check what his accountant sends back. One of his go-to prompts is basically just "what questions am I not asking that I should be asking?" which is honestly the most useful thing you could type into any AI tool.

The part that caught our attention is what happened when he started comparing his own AI-assisted tax prep against his accountant's work. He would bring the discrepancies back to his CPA and sometimes they would say yeah, good catch, you can do that. Other times they would explain why he couldn't. Either way he was having a better conversation than he would have had walking in cold.

His CPA Amanda Han actually validates the approach for the basics. AI is great at explaining what depreciation is or how an S corp works, she told Business Insider. But when it comes to something like "is an S corp right for me specifically," that still needs a human. The line is pretty clear and it applies to basically any professional service. AI can get you 80% prepared so the expert you're paying spends their time on the 20% that actually requires judgment.

The $40 a month thing is what makes this worth paying attention to. A part-time bookkeeper runs $250 a month minimum. A quarterly CPA consultation is $400 to $600 a pop. Ray isn't replacing his accountant, he's just showing up way more prepared, which means he gets more value out of every hour he pays for. And the same approach works whether you're running a cleaning company, a consulting practice, a restaurant, or really any small business where you're the one staring at the books.

The Formula

1. Gather your financial docs. Pull together last year's tax return, your recent bank statements, and any receipts or expense records you have. Even messy is fine.

2. Open Claude and give it context. Tell it your business type, how you're structured (sole prop, LLC, S corp), your rough annual revenue, and your main expense categories. This is how it stops giving you generic answers.

3. Ask it to find what you're missing. Upload your tax return or paste in your expense categories and ask "what deductions or tax strategies might I be overlooking?" Then ask "what questions should I bring to my accountant?"

4. Prep a one-page CPA cheat sheet. Take Claude's output and organize it into a short list of questions and flagged items. Bring this to your next accountant meeting instead of showing up empty-handed.

5. After your CPA meeting, close the loop. Go back to Claude with what your accountant said. Ask follow-up questions while the conversation is fresh. Save the whole thread so you're not starting from zero next quarter.

Have Claude Explain This to Me

Copy this prompt into Claude:

A small business owner was spending too much time Googling tax questions
and showing up unprepared to CPA meetings. He started using AI to review
his expenses, surface overlooked deductions, and generate specific
questions for his accountant, all for $40 a month.

Here's the basic approach from Thorium Valley:
- Give Claude your business structure, revenue range, and expense categories
- Upload or describe your financial docs and ask what you might be missing
- Generate a list of questions to bring to your next accountant meeting
- After the meeting, use Claude to follow up on what your CPA recommended

1. What's your business structure and roughly how much revenue are you
   working with, and how do you currently track your expenses?
2. What part of your finances takes the most time or feels like the
   biggest blind spot right now?"

stories.title: Clay's Team Built 80 AI Agents in a Week. Each One Took 5 Minutes.
stories.content:
Five minutes per agent, no code, no hand-holding.

Clay is, ironically, a go-to-market data platform. The company helps other teams automate manual data work but they were drowning in their own coordination overhead. Willie Yao, Clay's head of engineering, kept finding out about customer issues hours after they'd already escalated. Details lived in a Slack thread somewhere but he couldn't monitor every channel personally. Meanwhile Yash Tekriwal, who runs education and community, was spending hours each week digging through call transcripts looking for customer insights.

Both problems came down to the same thing. The information existed, it just sat there doing nothing.

Clay had already centralized everything in Notion, meeting notes, projects, docs, all connected to Slack and Google Drive. So when Notion rolled out Custom Agents, the team had a head start. All that context was already organized and waiting. Within a week they had 80+ agents running in the background across the entire company.

There were three that did a lot of the heavy lifting. First, the Meeting Classifier, which reads transcripts and figures out if something is a one-on-one, a team meeting, or all-hands, then files everything in the right place automatically. Second, the Incident Manager, which watches Slack for production issues and synthesizes what's happening, who's involved, and what to do next. "We realized that Custom Agents often do a better job when it comes to understanding what the root cause is," Willie said. And third, the Daily Briefer, which scans all of engineering's work every morning and pushes Willie a summary of active bugs, incidents, launches, and meetings to prep for. "People are surprised about the amount of context that I have," he said. "It's because I have this Custom Agent that's always looking out for me."

The setup was almost suspiciously easy. "I was shocked at how simple it was," Yash said. "I connected Slack, set up a prompt, and I was able to test the results in five minutes." And adoption spread entirely by word of mouth. Someone would ask Willie how he's tracking everything, he'd say Custom Agents, and that person would go build their own.

The real thing worth stealing here isn't the agents themselves but the pattern. If your team already keeps its work in one place, whether that's Notion or something similar, you're sitting on the same advantage Clay had. The meeting classifier idea works just as well for a project manager sorting client calls as it does for a community lead. The daily briefer is useful for anyone managing a team who's tired of manually piecing together what happened overnight.

The Formula

1. Pick one workflow that eats your time every week. Meeting notes piling up, status updates you compile by hand, messages you triage manually. Start with just one.

2. Make sure the information already lives in Notion. Agents need context to work with. If your meeting notes, project databases, or docs aren't in Notion yet, spend some time getting them there honestly.

3. Create a Custom Agent in Notion. Go to the Agents section in your sidebar, describe what you want in plain English, something like "read new meeting transcripts, classify them by type, and file them in the right database." Notion will generate the instructions and triggers for you.

4. Set a trigger and limit the access. Choose when the agent should run, like when a new page hits your meetings database or every morning at 9 AM. Only give it access to the specific pages and databases it actually needs.

5. Test it with real examples, then let it run. Trigger it manually a few times, check the output, adjust the instructions if something's off, and then turn it loose. Check back after a week to see if it's actually saving you time before building the next one.

Have Claude Explain This to Me

Copy this prompt into Claude:

A fast-growing startup had useful information scattered across Notion,
Slack, and Google Drive but no one could act on it fast enough. They
built 80+ Custom Agents inside Notion that automatically classify
meeting notes, monitor Slack for issues, and generate daily briefings,
each one set up in about 5 minutes with zero code.

Here's the basic approach from Thorium Valley:
- Identify one repetitive workflow you do manually every week
- Make sure the relevant info already lives in Notion
- Create a Custom Agent using plain English instructions
- Set a trigger (new database entry, schedule, Slack message) and
  limit the agent's access to only what it needs
- Test with real data before expanding

stories.title: She Mapped Every Task Her Marketing Team Does. 80% Could Be Done by AI.
stories.content:
Teresa Barreira is the CMO of Publicis Sapient, the tech consulting arm of ad giant Publicis. Three years ago she told her marketing team to start using AI and experiment with it. Six months later she checked in to see how their work had changed. And you probably already guessed it, nothing changed. They were all "using" AI in the sense that they'd ask it to help write emails or brainstorm headlines, but the actual workflows, the sequence of who does what and when and how many people touch something before it ships, were identical.

So she took a first-principles approach. Her team mapped every single function across the entire marketing org and catalogued over 700 tasks they perform daily. The results were kind of brutal. Between 80% and 90% of those tasks could be accelerated or fully handled by AI. About 40% could run end-to-end with AI agents and no human in the loop at all.

The most concrete example is campaign launches. Her team puts out about five campaigns a month, and getting one to market used to require around 50 handoffs, people talking to people, approvals sitting in queues, files bouncing between tools. After redesigning the process around what AI could handle, they got it down to 11 steps.

The part that actually matters though is what she did next. She rewrote job descriptions for every function to focus on the 20% of work that only humans can do. Judgment, intuition, pattern recognition, the ability to go against the grain when the data says one thing but your gut says another. As Barreira put it, "AI is not going to be as brave as humans are."

This approach works whether you run a marketing team of 50 or you're one person trying to figure out where AI fits into your day. The exercise is the same. Write down what you actually do, be honest about how much of it is just coordination and production, and you'll probably find the ratio isn't that different from hers.

The Formula

1. Open a Google Sheet and list every task you do in a week. Column A is the task, Column B is who does it, Column C is how often, Column D is roughly how long it takes. Spend some time filling this in honestly. Don't write what your job description says, write what you actually do.

2. Score each task for AI-readiness. Add a Column E and mark each one as "AI can do this," "AI can help with this," or "only a human can do this." Be ruthless. If the task is mostly copying information between tools or following a checklist, it's probably in that first bucket.

3. Find your 50-to-11 moment. Pick the workflow with the most handoffs or steps and sketch out what it would look like if AI handled the parts you just flagged. You're looking for the steps where a person is basically acting as a middleman between two systems.

4. Rebuild one workflow first. Use Zapier to connect the tools involved and let it handle the routing and notifications automatically. Don't try to automate everything at once. Get one workflow running cleanly and learn from it.

5. Rewrite your own job description around the 20%. Once you see what AI can take off your plate, define what you should actually be spending time on. That's the whole point.

Have Claude Explain This to Me

Copy this prompt into Claude:

A CMO at a major consulting firm found that her team was using AI but
hadn't changed any of their actual workflows. She mapped all 700+ daily
tasks across her marketing org and discovered 80-90% could be accelerated
by AI, with 40% running fully autonomously. She then cut campaign launches
from 50 handoffs to 11 steps and rewrote every job description around the
20% of work only humans can do.

Here's the basic approach from Thorium Valley:
- List every task you do in a week in a spreadsheet with who does it,
  how often, and time spent
- Score each task as "AI can do this," "AI can help," or "human only"
- Find the workflow with the most handoffs and redesign it with AI
  handling the flagged steps
- Use Zapier to connect your tools and automate routing and notifications
- Redefine your role around the work that actually requires human judgment

Thorium Valley and heard you're trying to figure out which parts of your
work AI can actually take over. Could I get a little more context on:
1. What's your role and what does a typical week look like for you in
   terms of the types of tasks you spend the most time on?
2. What's the workflow that frustrates you the most right now, the one
   with too many steps or too many people involved before something
   actually gets done?"
